docs.title: FYP26 — AI agents in the biosciences
docs.text:
Your task in this project is to design a degron tagging approach for a phosphatase gene, and to compare your own design with one produced by an AI agent. You will learn some basic biological concepts — gene targeting, CRISPR, induced degradation, phosphatases — and in parallel get exposed to agentic AI, its powers and its limitations.

AI is sold as a research assistant. How good is it actually, on real scientific work?

Nobody can answer that without a ground truth — a set of answers worked out carefully by a person, against which a model can be scored. Producing that ground truth is your project.

You are not using AI. You are measuring it.

The week 1 lecture, in full

Download the introduction slides (PowerPoint, 39 slides) — the whole project in one place: the biology, the design decisions, how the agents are run and how any of it gets scored.

Everything on this site is somewhere in that deck. Come back to it when a phase opens and you want to see where the piece you are working on fits.

docs.title: What you will do
docs.text:
The project is structured in four phases to take you step by step through the different tasks. All five of you follow the same progression. The only thing that differs is which phosphatase you work on. You each get a different one, and everyone also does one shared protein. You find out which in week 4, when phase 1 rolls out on 27 October.

The project schedule lists the meetings, submissions and presentations. Phase 3 ends with the thesis.

Phase What Weeks Ends with 0 · Background Degron tags, agents and their connection to your phosphatase alongside the project combined background/protein presentation after Christmas, date and format to be confirmed 1 · Literature Evaluate agents; assemble tagging evidence and interpret supplied isoform/structure data 4–9 abstracts 10 Nov; full-text reference 17 Nov; design evidence 1 Dec; protein intro after Christmas 2 · Cloning Design the guide and donor, then compare with the cloning agent from 1 Dec human design presentation 8 Dec; comparison review 15 Dec 3 · Analysis Score the models against your annotations; write up → the thesis

Eleven weeks this term; the write-up is yours to pace over the vacation. The project schedule has the detail. Meetings are Tuesdays at 1 pm.

You answer first. Your answers are then locked, and only afterwards do the same questions go to the AI agents. Your work is the measuring stick, so it cannot be contaminated by seeing the model's answer.

docs.title: You get a Claude subscription
docs.text:
Paid for by the department through Claude for Science, with a proper introduction to Claude Code. You will use it for reading, for code, for drafting, and for running your own agent over your gene.

Independent references come first: the 50 abstracts are due before the 10 November meeting, when accounts are issued. You then independently extract three full-text papers for 17 November, without AI or model answers despite having agent access. Lock the references before running the evaluations. Why.

docs.title: Why everyone does the shared protein too
docs.text:
Five people answering identical questions on one protein shows how much two careful humans disagree. Without that number, "the agent scored 0.7" means nothing — there is no scale to read it against.

It was picked as the one protein with a rich literature on both halves of the question: it has been degron-tagged and it is a well-known target for chemical degraders. A control with a thin answer on either half would waste the exercise.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Read this page.
  2. Open Phase 0 and read the four background pages filed under it — about forty minutes, and everyone reads the same four.
  3. Begin the protein reading and abstract work. Bring questions to the 3 November practice session; the combined background/protein presentation is after Christmas.

Do not read this site front to back. It is built to be visited, and each phase opens when you reach it.

docs.title: Protect the comparisons
docs.text:
• Independent answers first. Agent access on 10 November does not permit AI assistance on the three full-text reference papers. Complete these before seeing the extraction agent's output.
  • Keep originals. Student and supervisor records remain separate. Resolve disagreements in an adjudicated copy and lock it before the evaluation runs.
  • Check before applying. If the 24 November review finds material failures, agree a narrower or manually checked workflow rather than trusting its output.
  • Human cloning design first. Save the design presented on 8 December before inspecting the cloning agent's design. Document later revisions and agree the comparison criteria before reporting scores.

docs.title: Keep the workload bounded
docs.text:
The full-text evaluation is three papers per student, not ten. It is a small pilot, not a comprehensive benchmark. Suitable papers can also contribute to the gene-specific analysis; do not duplicate the extraction.

Bring your current work, one unresolved question and any blocker to each meeting. Export annotations before leaving the tool. If the schedule becomes unmanageable, agree a reduced scope with your supervisor rather than rushing the independent reference work.

docs.title: Degraders vs degrons
docs.text:
Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. Read it once, early.

Two ways to destroy a chosen protein on demand. Same machinery, opposite strategies. You work on the genetic one, and the contrast with the chemical one is the best framing device you have.

docs.title: The shared problem
docs.text:
You want to know what a protein does. Three classic options, three problems:

Approach Problem Inhibitor only works if the protein has a druggable pocket. Most don't Knockout kills the cell if the gene is essential RNAi / antisense acts on RNA, so the phenotype waits for existing protein to turn over

All three leave you unable to ask "what happens in the first hour after this protein disappears?"

docs.title: The shared solution
docs.text:
Hijack the ubiquitin–proteasome system — the cell's own machinery for tagging proteins with ubiquitin and shredding them. Redirect it at a protein of your choosing.

Then the two approaches fork.

docs.title: Chemical: degraders
docs.text:
Make a molecule that physically brings the target and an E3 ligase together. The ligase tags the target, the proteasome destroys it.

  • PROTAC — two ligands and a linker. One end binds the target, the other the ligase.
  • Molecular glue — a single small molecule that makes the two surfaces stick.

No genetic modification. Works on unmodified cells, patients included — which is why this is a drug modality.

But you need a ligand that binds your target. If nothing binds it, you have nothing to build from.

docs.title: Genetic: degrons — what you will design
docs.text:
Edit the gene so the protein is made with a degron attached — a tag that can be switched into a destruction signal. Add the trigger molecule and the tagged protein disappears in minutes.

  • AID / AID2 — plant auxin system, triggered by auxin or 5-Ph-IAA
  • dTAG — FKBP12(F36V) tag, triggered by dTAG-13
  • SMASh, deGradFP — other routes to the same end

Works on any protein, ligand or not, because you attach the handle yourself.

But you have to edit the genome. No use in a patient, and it takes months of cloning per target.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Degrader (chemical) Degron (genetic) Genome edited? No Yes Needs a ligand? Yes No Works in patients? Yes No Time to a new target months of chemistry months of cloning Primary use therapy, and chemical biology lab tool for essential genes Off-target risk other proteins degraded tag perturbs the protein Signature failure hook effect leaky basal degradation

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
• No ligand for your protein? Degron.
  • Can't or won't modify the genome? Degrader.
  • Want a therapy? Degrader.
  • Need clean acute loss of an essential gene in a cell line? Degron.

Getting that crisp is one of the most useful things your presentation can deliver.

docs.title: Where the boundary bites
docs.text:
You will meet papers that sit between the two, and you will have to decide what to call them. A bioPROTAC is a genetically encoded protein that acts like a PROTAC. A degron appearing in a molecular glue paper usually means the short natural sequence the ligase recognises, not an engineered tag.

Read what was actually done, not which words appear.

docs.title: Evaluating agents
docs.text: Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. It is the short version of the problem this whole project exists to attack.

docs.title: The question that sounds easy
docs.text:
Is the agent any good?

You cannot answer that by looking at its output and nodding. A confident, well-written, completely wrong answer looks exactly like a confident, well-written, correct one — that is what these models are good at. To say anything at all you need something to compare the answer against.

That something is a ground truth: a set of answers worked out carefully by a person, in advance, against which the agent can be scored.

Producing one is the hard part, and it is your project. You are not using AI. You are measuring it.

docs.title: Two ways people score agents
docs.text:
The literature splits, and the split matters because the two approaches disagree about what counts as doing well.

Verifiable answer. Ask something with one checkable answer — a number, a name, a sequence — and compare. Cheap, repeatable, and a script can do the marking. The catch is that only narrow questions have single right answers, so you end up measuring the narrow things because they are the measurable ones.

Trajectory and rubric. Judge how the agent worked, not just what it concluded. Did it check the thing it claimed to check? Did it notice the failed tool call? This captures far more of what you actually care about, but it needs a human to judge, and humans disagree with each other.

This project uses both, which is why some of your answers are single fields and some are judgements about a design.

docs.title: Why agents are harder to score than models
docs.text:
A chatbot gives one answer. An agent runs a loop, and the loop adds:

  • a different number of steps on every run
  • tool calls that fail, and may or may not be retried
  • context that drifts as the transcript grows

So the same agent, asked the same question twice, does not do the same thing twice. One run is an anecdote. Any claim about an agent needs repeated runs, and a statement of how much it varied.

docs.title: What makes a measurement trustworthy
docs.text:
Three things, all of which you will meet again in phases 1 and 2:

You answer first Your answers are locked before the agent sees the question. Otherwise you are marking the agent against something it influenced Honest gaps count "Not stated" is a real answer. If the source never said it and the agent invents it, you have caught something — but only if your own answer admits the gap Evidence, not memory Every answer carries the text or command it came from, so somebody else can check it

docs.title: Where this goes next
docs.text:
In phase 1 you build a ground truth by hand and discover how often two careful people disagree. In phase 3 you turn all of it into numbers.

For now you only need to understand the problem well enough to write about it — and to see why "the agent scored 0.7" means nothing on its own.

docs.title: Gene targeting
docs.text: Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. It explains how a tag gets onto a protein in the first place — the thing you will design in phase 2.

docs.title: Why you have to edit the genome
docs.text:
A degron tag is not a drug you add to cells. It is a piece of protein, and the only way a cell makes it is if the instructions are in the gene.

So to tag a protein you have to change the DNA: find the gene, and insert the tag sequence at one end of it, in the right place, without breaking anything else. That is gene targeting.

Do it properly and every copy of the protein the cell makes from then on carries the tag. That is what makes it an endogenous tag, and it is the whole point — the protein stays under its own control, at its own level, in its own places.

docs.title: Two things you need
docs.text:
A cut, at exactly the right position in the genome.

A template, telling the cell what to put there.

Neither works without the other. A cut on its own gets repaired badly. A template on its own is ignored.

docs.title: The cut: CRISPR
docs.text:
Cas9 is a protein that cuts DNA. On its own it has no idea where to cut.

You give it a guide RNA — about 20 bases that match the sequence you are aiming at. The guide finds its match by base pairing, Cas9 cuts there, and you have a double-strand break where you wanted one.

There is one constraint that catches everyone out. Cas9 will only cut next to a short motif called a PAM — for the common Cas9, the letters NGG. No PAM, no cut, however good your guide is. So you cannot cut anywhere you like; you can only cut near a PAM, and that is often the thing that decides your design.

docs.title: The repair: two paths, and you want the rarer one
docs.text:
Cells hate double-strand breaks and fix them immediately, by one of two routes.

NHEJ — non-homologous end joining Shoves the ends back together. Fast, always available, and sloppy — it often inserts or deletes a few bases. This is how you make a knockout HDR — homology-directed repair Copies from a template with matching ends. Accurate, but only works in dividing cells and is much rarer. This is how you make a knock-in

You want HDR. The cell mostly wants NHEJ. Much of the practical difficulty of knock-in work comes from that disagreement.

docs.title: The template: your donor
docs.text:
The donor is the DNA you supply as the template. It has three parts:

  • a left homology arm — sequence matching the genome on one side of the cut
  • the cassette — what you are inserting: the tag, usually with a linker and often a selection marker
  • a right homology arm — matching the genome on the other side

The arms are what tell the cell where this belongs. HDR recognises them, copies the whole middle section in between, and the cassette ends up at the cut site.

docs.title: Which end of the protein
docs.text:
A degron tag goes at one end of the protein — the N-terminus (where the protein starts) or the C-terminus (where it ends). In the gene, that means inserting either just after the start codon or just before the stop codon.

Choosing between them is a biology question, not a cloning one. A tag can block a binding site, hide a signal that sends the protein somewhere, or sit on top of a modification the cell uses to control the protein. Which end is safe depends on what is at each end of your protein — which is exactly what you will spend phase 1 finding out.

docs.title: The thing that goes wrong most often
docs.text:
The reading frame.

The cell reads DNA in three-base codons. Your tag has to be joined to the protein-coding sequence so that it continues in the same frame — otherwise every codon after the join is read wrong and you get nonsense.

One base out is enough to ruin it. And the construct will look perfectly fine on a map, because nothing about the sequence says "this is in the wrong frame" until you translate it.

That is the single most common error in this kind of design. In phase 2 you will be designing against it deliberately.

docs.title: Where this goes next
docs.text:
Phase 1 tells you which end of your protein a tag can go on. Phase 2 is where you design the guide and the donor to put it there.

You do not need the details yet. You need to understand that the design has a small number of parts, each of which has to be exactly right, and that "looks right" is not the same as "is right".

docs.title: How you are marked
docs.text:
Read this in week 1, not week 11. Students calibrate effort to what they believe is assessed; if that is invisible you will guess, and usually guess wrong.

This page is the policy — what is looked at, and what is not. The exact weights come from the FYP marking scheme and are confirmed at supervision.

docs.title: What is assessed everywhere
docs.text:
Component What good looks like Rigour of the ground truth Consistent conventions, honest gaps, evidence that verifies, ambiguities logged as you met them Quantitative analysis Appropriate statistics, human agreement reported as context rather than an accuracy ceiling, uncertainty stated Interpretation You can say what each number means and what it does not Methods transparency Someone else could repeat this from your write-up Presentation and communication Thesis and talk are clear

Ground-truth rigour carries the largest weight. It is the part nobody can do for you and the part everything downstream depends on.

docs.title: What is not assessed
docs.text:
• Whether the models do well. Not your doing, and a model failing informatively makes a better thesis than one that quietly succeeds.
  • Volume. Careful and smaller beats rushed and larger. If the timeline slips we scale the work down, not the care.
  • Whether you wrote the analysis code yourself. See below.

docs.title: On using AI
docs.text:
You have an account from 10 November, and using it is expected — for reading, for code, for drafting, for running your own agent over your gene.

One exception: independent reference-building. Do not use AI to produce, summarise or check the human answers used to evaluate an agent. This applies to both abstract and full-text reference annotations, until they are locked. Those judgements are the measurement. Why.

What is assessed is not whether you used AI. It is whether you can specify what you need, check that what came back is right, and interpret the result.

Keep a log of what you asked for, what came back, and what you had to fix. Include it as an appendix. It is evidence of the skill being assessed, and usually the most honest thing in the thesis.

docs.title: When things are due
docs.text: See the project schedule. The 3 November session is for abstract questions and full-text practice, not a presentation or written hand-in. The combined background and protein introduction is after Christmas; its date, length and written format will be confirmed.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text: • 24 October 2026: Clarified independent-reference AI restrictions and that human agreement is not a model accuracy ceiling.

docs.title: What an AI agent is
docs.text: Everyone on FYP26 reads this page. Your questions go to an agent twice — once with nothing but its own knowledge and a shell, once with the tools we have built for the job. The contrast between those two is the experiment.

docs.title: Chat vs agent
docs.text:
A chatbot answers. You give it text, it gives you text back.

An agent acts. Given a goal, it decides what to do next, uses tools — running code, reading files, searching — looks at the results, and decides again. It loops until it thinks it is done.

The difference is the loop, and the loop is what makes agents both useful and hard to measure.

docs.title: Why the loop is hard to measure
docs.text:
Add a loop and you add:

  • tool calls that fail and get retried
  • a different number of steps on every run
  • context that drifts as the conversation grows

Any of those changes the answer. Run the same agent on the same question twice and you will not get the same transcript — which is why a single run is an anecdote rather than a measurement.

docs.title: The harness
docs.text:
The model is only half of an agent. The other half is the harness — the tools it can call, the instructions telling it how to work, the files it can see. Same model, different harness, and you get a different agent.

That is what this course measures.

docs.title: The two arms on this course
docs.text:
Bare the agent with its own knowledge and a shell, nothing else. It can reason and it can run commands, but it has no route to your databases and no instructions about your problem Equipped the same agent, same model, plus the tools and instructions we have built for degron design

Only the harness changes. That is the point: anything the two arms disagree about is attributable to the tooling, not to the model having a better day.

Its headline measurements are things only a loop can produce:

  • turns to completion — how many steps it took
  • tool-error rate — how often a tool call failed
  • recovery — whether it noticed a failed call, or carried on regardless
  • assertion without action — the agent claiming it ran a check it never ran

The last one is the most interesting failure mode on the course, and it is invisible without a loop — a single answer gives you no way to tell a checked claim from an unchecked one.

docs.title: Why both arms are recorded the same way
docs.text: Bare versus equipped, on the same questions, with the same model. For that comparison to mean anything, both runs have to be written down in the same format, so that a difference in the numbers is a difference in the agents and not in how you took notes.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
Building Effective Agents — Anthropic. Short, and the standard reference.

Components of a Coding Agent — Sebastian Raschka. The same loop taken apart piece by piece.

docs.title: Your Claude account
docs.text:
You each get a Claude subscription, paid for by the department through Claude for Science, and a proper introduction to Claude Code.

You get it on 10 November, the morning your annotations are due. From then on you need it: the session that day sets you up with Claude Code, and the week after you use it to run the literature analysis over your own phosphatase.

docs.title: Where you must not use it
docs.text:
Independent reference annotations used to evaluate an agent.

This includes the fifty abstracts and any later manual full-text reference set. Do not use AI to summarise, interpret or check those items before the reference is locked. Also keep model answers out of human adjudication.

Outside that reference-building work, use it for reading, searching, coding, drafting and running your agent. Follow the source restrictions for each task: abstract-only answers must be locked before you read the full papers.

docs.title: Why that one place
docs.text:
You are building the measuring stick.

The project rests on a single claim: that a careful person, working from the evidence, produces answers good enough to judge a machine against. Produce those answers with the machine and you have measured nothing — the model agrees with itself, you report 0.9, and the number means nothing at all.

It is the same reason a scale is calibrated with a known weight rather than with whatever happens to be sitting on it.

Plan several annotation sessions, not a single last-minute block. Time a few items after practice, then budget for the remainder, checking and export.

The deadline comes before the account session to help keep this sequence clear. The restriction applies to all AI tools, including any you already have—not just the account we provide.

What if I slip?

Tell us, and say which items were affected. Nothing bad happens — we drop those items or mark them, and the dataset stays honest.

Reporting this early lets us protect the comparison. Keep the original record and explain what happened; your supervisor will agree how to handle the affected items.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text: A Claude account Standard seat, yours for the project and the write-up Claude Code the agent, on your own machine, with a hands-on session A demonstration a real run on screen, including what goes wrong

docs.title: Keep a log
docs.text:
From the moment you start using it: what you asked for, what came back, and what you had to fix.

It goes in the thesis as an appendix, and it is usually the most honest thing in it. What is assessed is not whether you used AI — it is whether you can specify what you need, check that what came back is right, and interpret the result. The log is the evidence of that, and it is much easier to keep as you go than to reconstruct in week 11.

See How you are marked.

docs.title: What the demonstration is for
docs.text:
Later in the project you analyse what an agent actually did — how many steps it took, which tool calls failed, whether it noticed, whether it claimed to check something it never checked.

You cannot analyse that having never watched it happen. So you see a real run, on a worked example, with the transcript on screen. Take notes: the things that go wrong are the interesting part, and they go wrong in ways you would not guess.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text: • 24 October 2026: Clarified that independent full-text reference work also excludes AI; replaced the fixed annotation-time estimate with session-based planning and clarified how to report accidental exposure.

docs.title: Writing style contract
docs.text:
For whoever writes or edits these pages — including AI assistants, which default to comprehensive when teaching material needs to be sparse.

The 2025 cohort was given PDFs of long markdown notes. The format was not the problem; the register was. Reference prose dressed as instruction serves nobody.

docs.title: Site structure — shared vs project
docs.text:
docs/
  index.md              course landing; the four projects and what they share
  course/               everyone reads; must be project-neutral
  projects/<slug>/      one section per project, do/ lookup/ understand/ ...
  meta/                 this contract

Two rules, and they are the ones most likely to be broken by an assistant adding "just one more page":

  1. Nothing in course/ may address a single student or name one project's fields. If a sentence only makes sense to the literature student, it belongs in projects/literature/. Cross-project examples are fine; second-person instructions to one student are not.
  2. Nothing in projects/ may restate a course/ page. Link to it. A project's marking page carries its weights only; the policy lives in course/how-you-are-marked.md.

One repo, not one per project. The shared pages would drift within a term, and the whole design is a comparison between the projects — students need to be able to read across.

docs.title: Hard limits
docs.text: Section Limit do/ task cards 2 screens. If it doesn't fit, the task is too big — split it lookup/ pages 1 screen, or a table of any length understand/ pages 3 screens reference/ no limit; nobody reads these front to back

docs.title: The four registers, never mixed on one page
docs.text:
• do/ — imperative, one sitting's work, gated by week.
  • lookup/ — terse, tabular, for glancing at mid-task.
  • understand/ — narrative, read once, explains why.
  • reference/ — the full spec, for settling a dispute.

A student halfway through abstract 47 needs a one-page table, not paragraph six of section eight. That is the whole point of the split.

docs.title: Every task card has these six headings, in this order
docs.text:
## Goal
One sentence.

## Time
Realistic, not optimistic.

## Before you start
What must already be true.

## Steps
Numbered. Imperative. One action each.

## Done when
Explicit and checkable.

## If you get stuck
Three escalation steps, then email.

"Done when" is not optional. The most common student question is not "how?" but "is this right, and can I move on?" — and verbose prose is silent on exactly that.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Worked example before rule, never after. Nobody learns annotation from a rulebook. Show the JSON, then explain it.
  • Table over prose for anything enumerable.
  • No preamble. Delete "In this section we will…", "It is important to note that…", "As discussed above…".
  • Second person imperative. "Copy the span", not "the span should be copied".
  • One idea per numbered step. If a step has an "and" in it, split it.
  • Name the trap. Where students predictably go wrong, say so directly and say what to do instead.
  • No hedging. If something is genuinely uncertain, say what to do about the uncertainty.

docs.title: When you change a page
docs.text: Anything a student may have already acted on — the schema, the corpus, the annotation rules — gets a dated line in the changelog at the bottom of that page. Silent edits break the audit trail that the frozen corpus_version and schema_version exist to provide.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Explain how degron tagging and agentic AI connect to your phosphatase project. Develop that explanation as you read, evaluate agents and plan the cloning.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
Read during term; give one combined background and protein presentation after Christmas. The date, presentation length and written format will be confirmed. This replaces the separate background and phosphatase presentation tasks; it is not an additional assignment.

There is no presentation or written hand-in on 3 November. That session is for abstract questions and full-text practice. See the project schedule.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Read the background pages on AI agents, evaluating agents, degrons and degraders and gene targeting.

Use the reading list, the shared Zotero library and the supplied literature for your protein. Keep useful references and questions as you go; you do not need a finished talk now.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read about degron tags and agentic AI alongside the practical project work.
  2. Connect those methods to your phosphatase: its function, partners and what acute depletion could reveal.
  3. Keep concrete examples from the literature and your project, including agent errors and how you checked them.
  4. After Christmas, combine the background and protein story into one presentation, with supporting writing in the format agreed at supervision.
  5. Explain what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain.

docs.title: What to cover
docs.text:
Question Connect it to your project What does your phosphatase do? Its function, relevant partners and the biological question Why use a degron tag? What acute removal could reveal compared with knockout, knockdown or inhibition What can an agent contribute? The tools and workflow you used, not just a general definition of AI How did you evaluate it? Independent references, errors, checks and limits of your comparisons What does the evidence support? The case for your tagging design and the uncertainties you still need to resolve

Chemical degraders are useful context, but distinguish them from engineered degron tags. A presentation should make an argument, not list every paper read.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You connect degron biology and agents to your own phosphatase.
  • Your claims have identifiable sources or project evidence.
  • You explain both the value and limitations of the agent workflow.
  • You have delivered the combined presentation and supporting writing in the agreed format, without duplicating a separate protein presentation.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
Phase 1 runs alongside background reading. Submit 50 abstract classifications before 10 November and independently prepare three full-text reference papers for 17 November. Background reading should support the 1 December cloning decisions even though the presentation is later.

The 3 November practice uses papers outside the assigned abstract and full-text evaluation sets. Do not read your evaluation abstracts' full papers before their classifications are submitted and locked.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text: Revisit the background pages, bring a specific question to supervision and use examples from your practical work to make the concepts concrete. Keep existing drafts; they can feed the combined introduction rather than being rewritten as separate assignments.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text: • 26 October 2026: Moved the 3 November background presentation and written hand-in to a combined background/phosphatase introduction after Christmas. Date, length and written format remain to be confirmed. The freed session now covers abstract problems and full-text practice on separate papers.

docs.title: Reading for the presentation
docs.text:
Eight papers. That is the whole required list.

A thousand words is short, and four weeks is not long. Eight papers read properly and cited accurately will produce a better introduction than twenty skimmed. If you want more, the shared Zotero library has it — but read these first, and only go further if something has caught you.

Set Zotero up now, not in week 3

Accept the invitation, install Zotero and the browser connector, and point your reference manager at the group. You need references in the written introduction, and sorting this out while you are also writing is a miserable way to spend the week of the deadline.

docs.title: The seven
docs.text:
Degron tags — what you are putting on the protein

Covers 1 Nabet et al. 2018, Nat Chem Biol the dTAG system — what a degron tag is, and the figure showing a protein gone in 30 minutes 2 Crncec & Hochegger 2022, Methods Mol Biol degron tagging as an actual protocol, in RPE-1 cells, from this lab

Gene targeting — how it gets there

Covers 3 Doudna & Charpentier 2014, Science the CRISPR-Cas9 primer. One read gets you guides, PAMs and why a cut is only half the job 4 Choi et al. 2023, PNAS tagging proteins at their own locus with HDR donors. This is roughly what you design in phase 2

Agents, and whether anyone can tell if they are any good

Covers 5 Guo et al. 2026, Cell the overview: what "autonomous science" is being claimed, and where agents are actually being used in biology. Start the second half here 6 Nair et al. 2026, bioRxiv CompBioBench — AI agents turned loose on computational biology and scored against real answers 7 Kapoor et al. 2024, AI Agents That Matter why those scores are not to be trusted. The "agent benchmarks are broken" paper, and short 8 Gu et al. 2024, BLADE ground truth built from several independent experts, because experts disagree. The closest published thing to your shared protein

Papers 1–4 are the biology, and together they are one story: what the tag does, and how you get it onto the gene. Papers 5–8 are the measurement problem — 5 for what is being claimed, 6–8 for whether anyone can check it. Nothing here hands you the bridge between the two halves; that is the part that has to be yours.

Read the figures before the text, especially in 1, 2 and 4.

docs.title: Two short explainers, before paper 5
docs.text:
Neither is a paper and neither needs citing, but both are quicker than any of the above and will save you time.

Anthropic, Building effective agents what a tool-calling loop is, written plainly Raschka, Components of a coding agent the same loop taken apart piece by piece

docs.title: One thing to notice as you read
docs.text:
Paper 5 is in Cell. Papers 6, 7 and 8 are preprints — not peer reviewed. That gap is worth a sentence in your introduction: the overviews get refereed, while most of the work actually measuring these systems is still sitting on arXiv and bioRxiv, in a field moving faster than review can follow.

The split you will have to pick a side on

There are two ways to score an agent, and they disagree.

Verifiable answer — ask something with one checkable answer and compare. Cheap, reproducible, and only works on narrow questions. That is paper 6.

Trajectory and rubric — judge how the agent worked, not just what it concluded. Captures far more, but needs human judgement, which brings back exactly the annotator variance your ground truth is meant to pin down. That is paper 8.

This project does both, which is why your answers get locked and why everyone annotates the shared protein. Noticing that tension is a very good thing to put in your introduction.

docs.title: If you want more
docs.text: The Zotero library is filed by topic — Degron tags, Agentic AI, Evaluating agents. Nothing in there is required for phase 0. Add anything good you find; it is a group library, so what you add everyone gets.

docs.title: Degraders, for contrast
docs.text: PROTACs and molecular glues destroy a protein without modifying the gene. Same outcome, completely different method. The difference is set out in Degrons and degraders — read that page rather than duplicating it in a talk. You do not have to cover degraders in your introduction.

docs.title: Where to search
docs.text:
PubMed, and the papers that cite the eight above. A large part of phase 1 is discovering that keyword searching alone finds a surprisingly small fraction of the relevant literature — worth noticing early.

Note that papers 6–8 are not in PubMed. Agent evaluation lives almost entirely on arXiv and bioRxiv, which is the first thing this project will teach you about searching a young field.

docs.title: Phase 1 · Literature
docs.text:
Opens 27 October. Abstract classifications due 10 November. Three full-text reference papers ready for 17 November. Combined background/protein presentation after Christmas.

Read about your protein alongside the evaluation work. Finish the evidence needed for the cloning design by 1 December; the written introduction is part of the combined introduction after Christmas. Follow the project schedule for Tuesday meetings and preparation.

docs.title: The seven parts
docs.text:
Part numbers identify tasks, not seven consecutive weeks. In particular, Part 6's independent reference work starts on 10 November, so both abstract and full-text agents can be evaluated during 17–24 November.

Part Task Output and timing 1 · Your protein Read the supplied background literature Biological understanding now; combined background/protein presentation after Christmas, date, length and written format to be confirmed 2 · Abstract classification Independently classify 50 abstracts Submitted, locked JSON before the 10 November meeting 3 · Literature classification with an agent Run the classifier on the same abstracts after reference assembly and locking Saved predictions and run details, 17–24 November 4 · Agent evaluation Compare with the independent reference; investigate disagreements and screening errors Results and limitations for review on 24 November 5 · Gene-specific literature search Apply the reviewed screening workflow to your gene; check candidates and audit rejections Search record and candidate reading list, 24 November–1 December, subject to approval at the review 6 · Full-text agent evaluation Independently extract three papers, then compare the extraction agent against the locked reference Human records 10–17 November; combined reference on 17 November; evaluation runs 17–24 November 7 · Full-text tagging analysis Apply the evaluated workflow to relevant papers and verify its claims Tagging evidence, sources and uncertainties ready for cloning planning on 1 December

docs.title: Independent full-text reference · Three papers each
docs.text:
On 10 November, your supervisor introduces the assigned papers and recording format. Complete the independent extraction before the 17 November meeting. Record:

  • Protein and tag used.
  • Native-locus or ectopic expression strategy.
  • Tag position.
  • The experiment, if any, supporting retained protein function.
  • The location of supporting information in the paper or supplement.

Do this without AI or access to the extraction agent's answers, even though you receive an agent account on 10 November. Keep these records separate from your locked abstract classifications.

On 17 November, assemble the student and supervisor annotations. Preserve both originals, resolve disagreements in a separate reference and lock that reference before running the evaluations. This is a small pilot, not a comprehensive performance benchmark.

docs.title: From evaluation to your gene
docs.text:
Review both agents on 24 November. If the workflow is suitable, use it to search and analyse your gene's literature during the following week. Save the responses and verify the claims that will inform your design. If it fails, agree corrections, a narrower scope or manual checking before proceeding.

You also receive the isoform, modification and structure data on 24 November. Interpret these alongside the literature before the 1 December cloning planning session. These data are supplied; you do not need to build the underlying database yourself.

Suitable evaluation papers can also contribute to the gene-specific analysis; do not repeat the extraction. If your gene has no suitable precedent, your supervisor supplies practice papers for Part 6. Part 7 has no fixed paper quota: analyse the relevant evidence found. “No precedent found” is not evidence that tagging will fail.

docs.title: How this informs the design
docs.text:
Part 1 explains why the experiment is useful. Parts 2–7 establish what the literature workflow can do and what prior tagging experiments support. The fifty abstracts test a method; they need not concern your assigned gene. Why evaluate first?

Literature, isoforms, modifications and structures together inform Phase 2 · Cloning. No single source guarantees that a tag will work. Bring the evidence and remaining uncertainties to the design session, rather than an unverified agent recommendation.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Explain what your phosphatase does and evaluate whether acute degron-mediated removal would answer a useful biological question. A weak or conditional case is an acceptable conclusion if you explain the evidence.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Present after Christmas as part of the combined background and protein introduction. The date, length and written format will be confirmed; there is no separate protein presentation to prepare. Read during term so you can use the biology in the 1 December cloning session. The final writing can wait; the understanding needed for the design cannot. See the project schedule.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Know your assigned gene symbol. Revisit degrons and degraders if the difference between removing a protein and inhibiting it is unclear.

These are the five proteins we are studying:

Gene symbol Protein Subunit type PPP1CC PP1γ Catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 1 PPP2CA PP2A-Cα Catalytic α subunit of protein phosphatase 2A PPP4C PP4C Catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 4 PPP6C PP6C Catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 6 PPP2R2A PP2A-B55α Regulatory B55α subunit of protein phosphatase 2A

PPP2R2A is regulatory, not catalytic. Distinguish evidence about your specific subunit from evidence about the whole phosphatase complex.

Your supervisor will provide the literature in the shared Zotero library. Use this as the basis for your introduction. You may look for additional papers if you want to explore further, but an independent literature search is not required for Part 1.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the literature supplied for your protein in the shared Zotero library.
  2. Develop an argument addressing the questions below. Keep sources supporting your main claims.
  3. Connect it to degron tagging, agents and evidence from your project.
  4. Include it in the combined introduction and presentation after Christmas, in the format agreed at supervision.
Question What to look for What does it do in the cell cycle? Substrates, transitions and consequences of loss. Identify the relevant kinase relationship where known; do not force one if it is unclear. Which protein or complex is being studied? Distinguish your subunit from its family and holoenzyme. A paper about “PP2A” need not establish a role for your particular subunit. Why remove it acutely? A specific question about immediate effects, timing or adaptation that a chronic knockout or slow knockdown may not resolve. Why not use an inhibitor? Availability, selectivity and what inhibition would test. Removing a protein can affect scaffolding as well as catalytic activity, so the two approaches need not be equivalent. What remains uncertain? Missing evidence, competing explanations and conditions under which tagging would be worthwhile.

Draft the argument before making slides. Existing protein drafts can feed the combined introduction; do not create a duplicate submission.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You can explain your protein's role in one sentence, with any important qualification.
  • Your argument identifies a biological question, not just a technique you want to use.
  • You compare acute removal with knockout, knockdown or inhibition where relevant.
  • Your main claims have citations; gaps are labelled rather than filled by guesswork.
  • Your protein argument is incorporated into the combined background presentation and supporting writing in the agreed format.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text:
1. Check whether the review discusses your subunit, a family or the whole complex.
  2. Follow one relevant citation to a primary study to inspect the evidence.
  3. Write the unresolved question and bring it to supervision.

Email your supervisor if the uncertainty is blocking progress; you do not need to manufacture a positive case for tagging.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Classify 50 abstracts to create an independent reference for evaluating a classification-only model (Jev). These are a shared-method evaluation set, not necessarily papers about your phosphatase. Afterwards, apply the evaluated workflow to your own gene. Why this evaluation matters.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: The abstract JSON is due 10 November, before the agent session. Spread the work across several sessions. Full-text work comes after the abstract answers are submitted and locked. Part 6 starts on 10 November: independently extract three papers per student, ready for reference assembly on 17 November. The recording format is introduced on 10 November. Model evaluation runs follow reference locking, during 17–24 November. See the seven-part roadmap and project schedule.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Download your assigned S?_items.json file.
  • Complete the workshop, then compare with the solutions when invited.
  • Keep AI and full texts out of the independent abstract task.

docs.title: Classification options
docs.text:
Use exactly these labels. The same four fields are used for students and the classifier; no generated text, quotes, confidence ratings or other extraction fields are required.

Field Options is_tagging_paper yes, no, unsure tag_type AID, dTag, SMASH, bromo, other, multiple, unclear locus_strategy endogenous, exogenous, unclear terminus C-term, N-term, unclear
  • yes: the study attaches a degron or another tag to a protein.
  • no: it does not. A natural degron motif or small-molecule degrader alone does not count. Skip the other three fields.
  • unsure: the abstract does not settle whether tagging occurred.
  • yes and unsure both queue a paper for later full-text reading. Complete the other three fields using only the abstract.
  • AID includes AID2 and mAID; dTag covers dTAG; SMASH covers SMASh; bromo covers BromoTag.
  • other: a stated tag outside those families, including fluorescent or epitope tags. unclear: the category cannot be established from the abstract.
  • multiple: experimental use or comparison of more than one tag category, such as dTag and BromoTag. Background mentions do not count. AID and AID2 together remain AID.
  • endogenous: tagging at the native locus. exogenous: an ectopic expression construct, transfected or integrated. CRISPR alone does not prove endogenous tagging; exogenous does not require measured overexpression.
  • Use unclear when one option cannot represent the abstract, including mixed locus strategies or internal/mixed tag positions. Do not infer a terminus from what would make biological sense.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the annotation tool and load your assigned items file.
  2. Read the title and abstract; choose yes, no or unsure.
  3. For yes or unsure, classify tag type, locus strategy and terminus.
  4. Export after every session. Keep the downloaded JSON: browser storage is not a backup.
  5. Check that the tool reports 50/50 complete, then send the final export to your supervisor.

docs.title: Resume from a saved export
docs.text:
In the same browser, load the same assigned items file to resume browser-saved work. On another browser, or after clearing storage:

  1. Load your original S?_items.json file.
  2. Click Restore saved annotations and choose your latest answers export.
  3. Check the set and record count, then confirm.

Restore replaces current answers, rather than merging them. Export current work first if you need to keep it. Items absent from the backup become blank. Wrong sets and full-text records are rejected.

The new scheme is version 3. Old backups and browser records are not silently converted: keep them, but reclassify with the new options. Old browser records remain untouched in a separate storage key.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• All 50 items have a screening decision.
  • Every yes or unsure record has all three additional classifications.
  • Every no record omits the additional fields.
  • The export reports 50/50 complete.
  • You have sent the abstract JSON by 10 November and kept a local copy.
  • Your supervisor confirms receipt and locking before you open full texts or inspect model answers.

Full-text extraction uses a later, separate workflow. Function checks, degradation results, protein names and other detailed information are not part of this abstract classification task.

docs.title: Classifier instructions
docs.text: Supply the title and abstract only. Ask the classifier to select one of the exact labels listed above for each applicable field, using the same definitions. Run the three detail classifications only for yes or unsure. The runner—not the classifier—adds item ID, annotator identity, stage, timestamp and schema version. No text generation is needed. The repository file docs/phases/1-literature/reference/tagging-schema.json defines the saved format.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text: Use unsure for unresolved screening and unclear for unsupported detail classifications. Ask your supervisor about a convention if necessary; do not look up the paper or ask AI to resolve your independent abstract answer.

docs.title: Examples · Solutions and discussion
docs.text:
Open after thinking, discussing and recording your decisions. The worksheet contains the complete abstracts. Explanations below are teaching material, not required classifier output.

Draft — supervisor sign-off required

Agree uncertain conventions before the assigned fifty, especially the boundary between no and unsure and whether fusion names establish a terminus.

docs.title: Proposed classifications
docs.text:
Item / PMID is_tagging_paper tag_type locus_strategy terminus 1 / 38302485 yes AID unclear unclear 2 / 33979199 yes AID exogenous unclear 3 / 36409886 yes dTag unclear unclear 4 / 35089787 no — — — 5 / 41229306 unsure unclear unclear unclear

The dashes mean omit these fields, not an additional label. Items 1, 2, 3 and 5 proceed to later full-text reading; item 4 is screened out, subject to a separate audit of rejected papers.

docs.title: 1. A tag is clear; its locus is not
docs.text:
The medaka spindle abstract says “combining CRISPR knock-in with auxin-inducible degron technology”. This supports AID tagging but does not identify the integration site or terminus. CRISPR alone does not establish native-locus tagging. Do not assume Ran is the tagged target simply because it is the subject of the biological finding.

Discuss: what additional information would establish native-locus tagging?

docs.title: 2. CRISPR disrupts the locus; a construct supplies the tagged protein
docs.text:
The toolkit abstract describes “Sleeping Beauty transposon-based vectors for expressing auxin-inducible degron (AID)-tagged genes under the regulation of a tetracycline-controlled promoter”. The tagged protein comes from an ectopic construct: exogenous, not endogenous. Expression above native levels need not be demonstrated to use this label.

Discuss: would this be useful precedent for a native-locus design, and which conclusions would need qualification?

docs.title: 3. “Replaced” does not specify the method
docs.text:
The EBF1 abstract says “we replaced EBF1 by EBF1-FKBP^F36V in pro-B cells, allowing the rapid degradation by adding the degradation TAG13 (dTAG13) dimerizer”. This identifies dTag, but “replaced” does not distinguish native-locus tagging from knockout plus rescue.

The proposed conservative convention requires an explicit tag-position statement. A fusion name suggests an arrangement, but the later reference to the “C-terminal domain of EBF1” describes domain activity, not tag location. Agree the fusion-name convention before using it on the evaluation set.

Discuss: unclear can be a confident classification of insufficient information.

docs.title: 4. A natural degron is not an added tag
docs.text:
The Myc abstract describes “a phosphorylated Myc degron centered at threonine 58 (T58)” and “a second Fbw7 phosphodegron at Myc T244”. These are natural sequence motifs, not added tags: no. Omit the other fields.

This abstract screen does not establish that no tagged constructs appear anywhere in the full paper. That distinction is why rejected papers need an audit.

Discuss: does uncertainty concern the described mechanism, or merely the possibility that unreported methods contain tags?

docs.title: 5. Degradation chemistry and an unspecified construct
docs.text:
The FEM1B abstract mentions “the development of a stable construct of FEM1B”. The PROTAC context does not establish tagging, but the unspecified construct makes unsure a proposed screening answer: read the full text later to resolve whether it is tagged. The remaining categories are unclear.

The earlier excerpt-based example proposed no based on degradation chemistry alone. The complete abstract makes this a boundary case. If the supervisor chooses a convention that unspecified constructs are no, record it explicitly and apply it consistently; do not imply that no tag was used.

Discuss: what is the cost of admitting this paper versus missing a tagging precedent?

docs.title: Debrief
docs.text:
1. Identify one changed answer and the wording or rule responsible.
  2. Separate disagreements about the text from disagreements about conventions.
  3. Agree unresolved conventions with your supervisor.
  4. Distinguish unsure for screening from unclear for the other fields.

Keep practice separate from the evaluation set, then begin Part 2.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Based only on the complete PubMed abstracts on the worksheet, retrieved 24 October 2026; no full texts were consulted. Labels updated to the v3 classification-only scheme; the scientific interpretations remain proposed teaching answers pending supervisor sign-off.

docs.title: Two agents, two different questions
docs.text:
You want to know whether anyone has tagged your phosphatase, where the tag went and whether the tagged protein still worked. A broad search can return hundreds or thousands of papers, most of which will not answer that question.

Agent Task What a useful evaluation checks 1: abstract screening Recognise tagging information and recommend papers to open Does it miss tagging studies, admit irrelevant ones or invent details absent from the abstract? 2: full-text extraction Recover the tag, method, terminus and functional evidence Are its claims supported by the full text, including methods and supplements?

The fifty supplied abstracts test the first task. They are not necessarily about your gene. The full-text task needs separate manual full-text annotations: an abstract answer cannot establish what a full paper says. See Evaluating agents for the shared principles.

docs.title: Evidence, not plausible guesses
docs.text:
Abstracts often name a tag without specifying its location or integration method. If the source does not state a field, record not_stated—even when you have a plausible guess. For the screening decision, use cannot_tell when there is not enough information to decide whether tagging occurred.

Two recurring traps are natural degron motifs, which are part of a protein's sequence, and small-molecule degraders, which can remove a protein without adding a tag. Neither alone establishes a tagging study. Conversely, GFP or an epitope tag can supply relevant tagging precedent even when no degradation experiment was done.

“CRISPR” does not establish an endogenous tag. Even “knock-in” needs a stated integration site before you can assign the tag to the protein's native locus. Try the examples.

docs.title: How human answers become a reference
docs.text:
You and your supervisor annotate independently. Keep both original records. Before inspecting model answers, review disagreements together and record a separate adjudicated answer with its reasoning. If a rule needs clarification, record the change and apply it consistently.

Agreement is useful evidence of consistency, not proof of correctness or an accuracy ceiling. Two people can share a mistaken interpretation. Disagreements may reveal an unclear rule, missing evidence or a simple error; all are worth examining without treating them as personal failures.

docs.title: What the model's score can tell you
docs.text:
The supplied set contains roughly ten tagging abstracts and forty others, including deliberately difficult negatives. That is a test set, not a promise about the composition of your gene's literature. Its accuracy does not automatically transfer to a new search.

Report Why Sensitivity and specificity Separate missed tagging studies from irrelevant papers admitted. Counts and uncertainty With roughly ten positives, one missed paper changes sensitivity substantially. Uncertain decisions Report cannot_tell separately; agree how it is handled before scoring. Per-field agreement and unsupported values A correct screening decision can still come with an invented locus or terminus.

An all-negative screener could achieve about 80% accuracy here while missing every tagging study. That is why overall accuracy alone is misleading.

docs.title: Then apply the workflow to your gene
docs.text:
Keep the query, search date, candidate list and agent decisions. Read the full texts of yes and cannot_tell candidates. Also manually audit a sample of rejected abstracts, chosen before reading their full texts, to look for false negatives. Agree the sample size at supervision and report its limits; this is a check, not proof that nothing was missed.

For Agent 2, first produce and lock independent manual full-text annotations on an agreed evaluation subset, without AI. Record unavailable papers rather than treating them as negative results. Keep source locations for evidence in methods, results and supplements. Confirm the recording workflow and deadline with your supervisor before starting; do not reuse or overwrite the frozen abstract records.

A surviving tagged cell is useful precedent, but it does not establish normal protein function. Ask what was actually tested—activity, localisation, complementation or something else—and whether the organism, cell model, tag and expression context are relevant to your design.

The final claim should be “we found this evidence within this search”, not “nobody has ever tagged it” simply because the agent returned no candidates.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text: • 24 October 2026: Separated screening and full-text evaluation; clarified limits of accuracy and human agreement, independent reference construction and checks on rejected papers.

docs.title: Examples · Abstracts and questions
docs.text: Think → discuss → decide → compare. Work from the titles and abstracts on this page only. Do not use AI, open the full papers or read the solutions yet. These five practice items are separate from your assigned fifty.

docs.title: How the session works
docs.text:
1. Think individually. Read each abstract and record your answers with supporting words.
  2. Discuss in pairs or small groups. Compare decisions, especially where you disagree.
  3. Decide. Record a group answer and any unresolved uncertainty. Keep your original answer too.
  4. Compare when the tutor invites you. Open the separate solutions page.
  5. Reflect. Note one decision you changed and the evidence or convention that changed it.

docs.title: Questions for every abstract
docs.text:
Question Record Does the abstract describe protein tagging? yes, no, unsure What type of tag is used? AID, dTag, SMASH, bromo, other, multiple, unclear Where is the tagged construct expressed from? endogenous, exogenous, unclear Where on the protein is the tag? C-term, N-term, unclear

For no, skip the other three fields. Both yes and unsure trigger later full-text reading. Use unclear when the abstract does not establish a single category. Use multiple for experimental use or comparison of more than one tag category, not background mentions; AID and AID2 remain AID. other means a stated tag outside the listed families; it is not a substitute for missing information. See the classification rules for tag-family mappings and locus definitions.

Discuss supporting words and remaining questions orally; no quotes, confidence ratings or free-text fields are required in the classification output.

A blank grid to copy into your own notes:

Item Tagging? Tag type Locus strategy Terminus 1 2 3 4 5

Discussion notes are optional workshop aids, not scored output. There is no target number of yes answers: judge each abstract on its own evidence.

docs.title: Abstract 1
docs.text:
Ran-GTP assembles a specialized spindle structure for accurate chromosome segregation in medaka early embryos. Nat Commun, 2024. PMID 38302485.

Despite drastic cellular changes during cleavage, a mitotic spindle assembles in each blastomere to accurately segregate duplicated chromosomes. Mechanisms of mitotic spindle assembly have been extensively studied using small somatic cells. However, mechanisms of spindle assembly in large vertebrate embryos remain little understood. Here, we establish functional assay systems in medaka (Oryzias latipes) embryos by combining CRISPR knock-in with auxin-inducible degron technology. Live imaging reveals several unexpected features of microtubule organization and centrosome positioning that achieve rapid, accurate cleavage. Importantly, Ran-GTP assembles a dense microtubule network at the metaphase spindle center that is essential for chromosome segregation in early embryos. This unique spindle structure is remodeled into a typical short, somatic-like spindle after blastula stages, when Ran-GTP becomes dispensable for chromosome segregation. We propose that despite the presence of centrosomes, the chromosome-derived Ran-GTP pathway has essential roles in functional spindle assembly in large, rapidly dividing vertebrate early embryos, similar to acentrosomal spindle assembly in oocytes.

Discuss: which experimental details can you record directly, and which would you need to investigate further?

docs.title: Abstract 2
docs.text:
One-step multiplex toolkit for efficient generation of conditional gene silencing human cell lines. Mol Biol Cell, 2021. PMID 33979199.

Loss-of-function analysis is one of the major arsenals we have for understanding gene functions in mammalian cells. For analysis of essential genes, the major challenge is to develop simple methodologies for tight and rapid inducible gene inactivation. One approach involves CRISPR-Cas9-mediated disruption of the endogenous locus in conjunction with the expression of a rescue construct, which can subsequently be turned off to produce a gene inactivation effect. Here we describe the development of a set of Sleeping Beauty transposon-based vectors for expressing auxin-inducible degron (AID)-tagged genes under the regulation of a tetracycline-controlled promoter. The dual transcriptional and degron-mediated post-translational regulation allows rapid and tight silencing of protein expression in mammalian cells. We demonstrated that both non-essential and essential genes could be targeted in human cell lines using a one-step transfection method. Moreover, multiple genes could be simultaneously or sequentially targeted, allowing inducible inactivation of multiple genes. These resources enable highly efficient generation of conditional gene silencing cell lines to facilitate functional studies of essential genes.

Discuss: sketch the experimental strategy. Which words support each part of your sketch?

docs.title: Abstract 3
docs.text:
EBF1 is continuously required for stabilizing local chromatin accessibility in pro-B cells. PNAS, 2022. PMID 36409886.

The establishment of de novo chromatin accessibility in lymphoid progenitors requires the "pioneering" function of transcription factor (TF) early B cell factor 1 (EBF1), which binds to naïve chromatin and induces accessibility by recruiting the BRG1 chromatin remodeler subunit. However, it remains unclear whether the function of EBF1 is continuously required for stabilizing local chromatin accessibility. To this end, we replaced EBF1 by EBF1-FKBP^F36V in pro-B cells, allowing the rapid degradation by adding the degradation TAG13 (dTAG13) dimerizer. EBF1 degradation results in a loss of genome-wide EBF1 occupancy and EBF1-targeted BRG1 binding. Chromatin accessibility was rapidly diminished at EBF1-binding sites with a preference for sites whose occupancy requires the pioneering activity of the C-terminal domain of EBF1. Diminished chromatin accessibility correlated with altered gene expression. Thus, continuous activity of EBF1 is required for the stable maintenance of the transcriptional and epigenetic state of pro-B cells.

Discuss: did your group interpret any phrase differently? What evidence would settle the disagreement?

docs.title: Abstract 4
docs.text:
Two diphosphorylated degrons control c-Myc degradation by the Fbw7 tumor suppressor. Sci Adv, 2022. PMID 35089787.

c-Myc (hereafter, Myc) is a cancer driver whose abundance is regulated by the SCF^Fbw7 ubiquitin ligase and proteasomal degradation. Fbw7 binds to a phosphorylated Myc degron centered at threonine 58 (T58), and mutations of Fbw7 or T58 impair Myc degradation in cancers. Here, we identify a second Fbw7 phosphodegron at Myc T244 that is required for Myc ubiquitylation and acts in concert with T58 to engage Fbw7. While Ras-dependent Myc serine 62 phosphorylation (pS62) is thought to stabilize Myc by preventing Fbw7 binding, we find instead that pS62 greatly enhances Fbw7 binding and is an integral part of a high-affinity degron. Crystallographic studies revealed that both degrons bind Fbw7 in their diphosphorylated forms and that the T244 degron is recognized via a unique mode involving Fbw7 arginine 689 (R689), a mutational hotspot in cancers. These insights have important implications for Myc-associated tumorigenesis and therapeutic strategies targeting Myc stability.

Discuss: what is the relationship between the mechanism described and the screening question you are trying to answer?

docs.title: Abstract 5
docs.text:
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance-based fragment screen of the E3 ligase Fem-1 homolog B. Protein Sci, 2025. PMID 41229306.

Targeted protein degradation using PROTACs (PROteolysis TArgeting Chimeras) has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy, largely relying on a small number of E3 ubiquitin ligases such as CRBN and VHL. However, resistance, toxicity, and poor oral bioavailability limit the utility of PROTACs and highlight the need to expand the E3 ligase toolbox. Fem-1 homolog B (FEM1B) is a lesser-known E3 ligase that offers a promising alternative due to its broad expression and ability to recognize diverse degron motifs. Here, we describe the development of a stable construct of FEM1B, the results of a protein-observed NMR-based fragment screen using this construct, and the X-ray structures of some of the fragment hits when bound to the protein. From these results, new PROTACs utilizing FEM1B as the E3 ligase may be discovered, providing an alternative E3 ligase for targeted protein degradation.

Discuss: what does the abstract tell you about the experimental construct? What, if anything, remains unresolved for your screening decision?

docs.title: Before opening the solutions
docs.text: Check that you have recorded your individual and group decisions, evidence quotes and at least one question to discuss with the tutor. Then, when invited, compare with the solutions.

docs.title: Sources and changes
docs.text:
Full abstracts retrieved from PubMed by the five PMIDs above on 24 October 2026, using pubmed_fetch_articles. Superscript notation is represented in plain text as returned by the retrieval tool. No full texts were used.

  • 24 October 2026: Replaced the mixed examples-and-answers page with an answer-free workshop worksheet. Included complete PubMed abstracts rather than selected excerpts; moved teaching answers and their caveats to a separate solutions page.

docs.title: Phase 2 · Cloning
docs.text:
Plan on 1 December · Present on 8 December

Receive isoform, modification and structure data on 24 November. Combine these with verified literature evidence before the 1 December design session. Present your human design on 8 December, before the cloning-agent demonstration. See the project schedule.

Design the CRISPR guide and the Gibson knock-in donor that would put a degron tag on your protein, at a terminus justified by the literature, isoforms, modifications and structures.

docs.title: What you will produce
docs.text:
A terminus choice with the evidence behind it — precedent, modifications, isoforms A guide RNA with your reasoning about cut site and off-targets Homology arms the right length, ending exactly where they must A donor cassette, linkers and arms, assembled in frame

Prepare the human design in SnapGene and be able to defend each choice. Keep it independent of the cloning agent's proposed design. Preserve the version you present on 8 December before inspecting agent-generated designs.

docs.title: Then compare with the cloning agent
docs.text:
After the presentations on 8 December, your supervisor demonstrates the cloning agent with and without DNAgent. During the following week, run the comparison and use the agent to help work out how to quantify human–agent differences. Record the comparison criteria, checks and any changes to them; do not overwrite your original human design.

Bring the results so far and unresolved questions to the 15 December summary and review.

docs.title: What you are given
docs.text:
The modification, isoform and structure data for your protein. Mapping all of that is a database job rather than a judgement one, and it would eat the rest of your term.

Interpreting it is the work. A tag that blocks a phosphorylation site, or lands on a terminus that only one of three isoforms shares, is a tag that will waste a year at the bench.

docs.title: Name the trap in advance
docs.text:
The frame. The arm has to end exactly on a codon boundary, because the linker is fixed and will not absorb a slip.

An off-by-one here produces a construct that looks perfectly right on a map and translates into nonsense. It is the most common single error in this kind of design, and nothing about the sequence announces it — you only find it by translating and reading the protein.

docs.title: How this connects back
docs.text:
Your literature work told you whether anyone has done this before, at which terminus, and whether the protein still worked. This is where that becomes a decision.

If precedent exists, say why you are following or departing from it. If it does not, say what you are inferring from and how confident you are. A design with honest uncertainty stated is worth more than a confident one that hides its assumptions.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You have a guide, arms and a donor that assemble in frame.
  • You can say why that terminus and not the other one.
  • Someone can ask "what if the paper you based this on used an overexpression construct?" and you have an answer.
  • Your human design is preserved before comparison with the cloning agent.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text: • 26 October 2026: Moved cloning planning to 1 December, after gene-specific literature and supplied isoform/structure evidence. Human designs are presented on 8 December before the agent demonstration; comparison work follows for review on 15 December.

docs.title: Phase 3 · Analysis and write-up
docs.text:
Literature evaluations · 17–24 November

Assemble and lock the human references on 17 November, then run the evaluations and analyse the results for 24 November. Cloning-agent comparisons follow the human design presentations on 8 December, with summary and review on 15 December. See the project schedule.

From mid-November to the end of term, then the vacation at your own pace.

Score the model runs against your annotations, work out what the numbers mean, and write the thesis.

docs.title: What you are given
docs.text: Your locked answers from phases 1 and 2 The agent runs the same questions, answered twice — once by a bare agent, once by the same agent equipped with the tools built for the job Everyone's answers on the shared protein the five of you against each other

docs.title: The number that makes the rest readable
docs.text: The five sets of answers on the shared protein give inter-rater agreement — how much careful people disagree with each other on the same material. This is context for interpreting model scores, not an accuracy ceiling. People can share errors, and an agent can sometimes be right when a reader is wrong. Keep independent records, investigate disagreements and distinguish agreement with the reference from scientific correctness.

docs.title: Agent access and independent work
docs.text:
Accounts are issued on 10 November, with a hands-on session. Use the agent for analysis, code and later writing, but not for the three independent full-text reference papers prepared during 10–17 November. Reference answers must be locked before model output is inspected.

After the 8 December cloning-agent demonstration, use the agent to help develop a way to quantify human–agent cloning differences. Preserve the human design first, document the comparison criteria and retain the raw results.

Keep a log of what you asked and what you had to fix. It goes in as an appendix. See Your Claude account.

docs.title: Over the vacation
docs.text: Use the 15 December review to agree remaining analysis and a writing plan. Finish the protein introduction after Christmas; its exact deadline will be confirmed.
